documents.ruleTitle: Verb be in the present (am / is / are)
documents.rule: Use am with I, is with he/she/it/one person or thing, and are with you/we/they/plural subjects.
correctExamples: I am a student.
She is happy.
They are at home.
documents.explanation: The verb be changes form to agree with the subject. Questions and negatives also use the correct form of be.
documents.exerciseHint: Choose am, is, or are: They ___ my friends.

documents.rule: Use a before consonant sounds and an before vowel sounds (a book, an apple).
correctExamples: a university (y sound)
an hour (silent h)
a cat
documents.explanation: Choose a or an based on the next sound, not always the next letter.

documents.rule: With he/she/it in the present simple, add -s or -es to the base verb (go → goes, watch → watches).
correctExamples: She goes to the gym every day.
He watches TV in the evening.
documents.explanation: Habitual actions and facts in the present use the base verb, except third person singular which takes -s/-es.
documents.exerciseHint: She ___ (go) to the gym every day.

documents.rule: Use am/is/are + verb-ing for actions happening now or around now, and temporary situations.
correctExamples: I am reading a book right now.
We are watching a movie now.
She is studying this week.
incorrectExamples: I read a book right now.
We is watching a movie now.
documents.explanation: Time markers such as now, at the moment, and right now often signal the present continuous. The auxiliary must match the subject (I am, he/she/it is, you/we/they are).

documents.rule: For finished actions in the past, use past simple: add -ed to regular verbs (work → worked) or use the irregular past form (do → did).
correctExamples: He did his homework yesterday.
They played football last week.
documents.explanation: Past time expressions (yesterday, last night, ago) usually require past simple, not present or -ing forms.

documents.rule: Use was/were + -ing for an action in progress at a specific time in the past, often when another action interrupts it.
correctExamples: They were having dinner when I arrived.
I was studying at 8 p.m.
incorrectExamples: They have dinner when I arrived.
documents.explanation: Past continuous describes background or ongoing past actions; past simple often marks the shorter interrupting event.

documents.rule: Use have/has + past participle for experiences without a specific past time (I have never been to Paris).
correctExamples: I have never been to Paris.
She has visited London twice.
documents.explanation: Has goes with he/she/it; have with I/you/we/they. The main verb is the past participle (been, visited), not past simple.

documents.rule: Short adjectives: add -er (tall → taller). Long adjectives: use more + adjective (more interesting). Use than after the comparative.
correctExamples: She is taller than her sister.
This test is more difficult than the last one.
incorrectExamples: She is tall than her sister.
documents.explanation: Comparatives compare two people or things. Do not use the base adjective alone when comparing.

documents.rule: Must and have to express obligation; should gives advice. After modals, use the base verb without to (must go, not must to go).
correctExamples: You must wear a seatbelt.
You should practice every day.
documents.explanation: Modals are followed by the infinitive without to (except have to, which is a semi-modal phrase).

documents.rule: If + present simple, will + base verb — for real and likely future results.
correctExamples: If it rains, I will stay home.
If you study, you will pass.
incorrectExamples: If it will rain, I stay home.
If you will study, you pass.
documents.explanation: Do not use will in the if-clause for first conditional.

documents.rule: Form passive with the correct tense of be + past participle when the action is more important than who did it.
correctExamples: The report was written last week.
English is spoken in many countries.
incorrectExamples: English is speak in many countries.
documents.explanation: The passive focuses on the object or result; the agent is optional (by + person).

documents.rule: Use who for people, which for things, and that for both in defining clauses that identify the noun.
correctExamples: The student who passed the test is happy.
The book which I bought is useful.
documents.explanation: Relative pronouns connect extra information to a noun; choose who/which/that correctly.

documents.rule: Common routine verbs: get up, have breakfast, go to work/school, finish, relax. Collocations matter (have breakfast, not take breakfast).
correctExamples: I have breakfast at 7.
She goes to work by bus.
documents.explanation: Learn verbs with their typical partners (collocations) for natural English.

documents.rule: Phrasal verbs combine a verb + particle (look after, give up). Meaning is often idiomatic.
correctExamples: She looks after her brother.
He gave up smoking.
incorrectExamples: He gave smoking up completely wrong particle placement in some contexts.
documents.explanation: Treat phrasal verbs as single units; particle choice changes meaning.

documents.rule: Read the title and first/last sentences of paragraphs first to understand the main idea before details.
correctExamples: Skim the text, then answer main-idea questions.
documents.explanation: Gist questions ask about the overall message, not one isolated word.

documents.rule: When the answer is not stated directly, combine clues from the text with logical inference.
correctExamples: The text says she forgot her umbrella and it was raining — infer she may get wet.
incorrectExamples: Choose an answer with a word that appears in the text but does not answer the question.
documents.explanation: Inference items test understanding beyond exact words; eliminate options that contradict the passage.
